investigation.outcome: Retest the unresolved label from the familiar source as well.

options.label: No; source approval is still missing
options.feedback: Completed review does not replace the independent source policy.

options.label: Yes; a numerical reviewed target is enough
options.feedback: That would let the new contribution channel bypass the boundary this release promised.

connections.skill: Trace fitted results to exact inputs
connections.why: The record identity must survive filtering and fitting.
Expected bytes and familiar names do not establish truthful training labels.

reflection.prompt: Which approved-source compromise would this gate fail to detect?
reflection.carryForward: Record what the filter establishes, and keep independent evaluation outside the same contribution channel.

preparation.title: Inspect eligibility before seeing its fitted effect
preparation.challenge: Build one flag per proposed record, requiring both source approval and completed review.
preparation.why: This separates the release decision from the numerical effect of fitting.
hints: Both pieces of evidence must describe the same row.
A reviewed proposal from an unapproved source still needs a zero flag.

security-backdoor-evaluation.premise: The clean metric looked reassuring because it never asked about the changed input condition.

construction.title: Build a report that can expose conditional failure
construction.start: Keep clean correctness on one branch. On another, define the eligible pair set before counting target hits.
construction.outcome: A high clean score remains visible without excusing a measured failure on the declared condition.
hints: Keep clean accuracy and the conditional test on separate branches.
A target prediction counts as a newly induced failure only when its eligibility flag is 1. Keep the success count and the eligible-pair count visible beside the rate.

investigation.title: Clean predictions stay fixed while changed predictions become safe
investigation.question: Which evidence must change in the report?
investigation.outcome: Retest the all-target population so an empty denominator remains unavailable rather than zero.

options.label: The targeted-success count, not the unchanged clean accuracy
options.feedback: The observations differ only on changed inputs, so the two metrics must remain separate.

options.label: Only clean accuracy; one score is enough
options.feedback: The ordinary predictions did not change and cannot describe the newly tested condition.

connections.skill: Keep evaluation outside the contribution channel
connections.why: A conditional failure needs its own reviewed evidence rather than a reassuring training story.

connections.skill: Name the population behind a metric
connections.why: The new denominator is a specifically eligible paired subset.

reflection.prompt: Which additional evidence would distinguish an implanted condition from an ordinary model weakness?
reflection.carryForward: Preserve paired case identities, denominators and ordinary task quality when reviewing a repair.

preparation.title: Choose the eligible paired examples
preparation.challenge: Mark clean-correct non-target examples only when the supplied edit has been reviewed as label-preserving.
preparation.why: The denominator must be established before a target-hit rate can be interpreted.
hints: A true target-class example is not a newly induced target prediction.
An already incorrect clean prediction does not enter this lesson’s induced-failure denominator.

security-adversarial-threat-models.premise: The initial small test passed, but a deliberately selected allowed change reached a different side of the boundary.

construction.title: Build the model and the scope checks side by side
construction.start: Start with the weighted-sum classifier. Keep the change-budget, domain and fixed-coordinate checks on a separate branch before combining the report.
construction.outcome: A wrong prediction is interpreted under the exact capability we declared.
hints: First construct the two predictions from the actual vectors and fixed weights.
Inspect the scope checks separately from the predictions. If observed_failure is null, use the remaining fields to see whether the trial was excluded or the original prediction was already wrong.

investigation.title: The allowed first coordinate reaches 0.5
investigation.question: The changed vector reaches the cutoff, while the original was below it. Does this create a new failure under the stated change rules and true label?
investigation.outcome: Retest the larger out-of-budget change without counting it as an in-scope failure.

options.label: Yes; it is in scope and the original was correct
options.feedback: The supplied change respects the budget and fixed-coordinate rule while the model’s inclusive cutoff now predicts 1.

options.label: No; the clean test had passed
options.feedback: The clean result says nothing about this additional allowed input.

connections.skill: Follow a weighted sum into a decision
connections.why: The familiar threshold now gives a visible decision boundary.
The capability checks define which prediction changes answer this experiment’s question.

reflection.prompt: Which claim would remain untested even after every supplied case passes?
reflection.carryForward: Record the capability, label assumptions and search coverage beside each robustness result.

preparation.title: Decide whether the supplied trial is in scope
preparation.challenge: Combine the size limit, fixed-coordinate rule and public domain checks into one flag of 0 or 1.
preparation.why: We must know what capability a trial represents before interpreting its failure.
hints: A permitted size does not allow a change to a protected coordinate.
The epsilon value goes before the measured largest change in a Threshold gate.

security-prediction-api-controls.premise: A request-count limit looked effective until batching changed the work inside one message.

construction.title: Reserve the actual prediction work
construction.start: Count the requested rows against the caller allowance. In another branch, calculate their estimated compute cost against global capacity. Require both checks before returning a public label.
construction.outcome: A batch cannot obtain a prediction merely because it fits one of the two independent allowances.
hints: Subtract prior use separately from each allowance.
Require both capacity flags, then pass the result into the public-label component. A denied request should not expose its internal score.

investigation.title: One envelope now carries 6 rows
investigation.question: The caller has 5 rows left. Does the single envelope fit this policy?
investigation.outcome: Retest the independently exhausted global budget before returning any public label.

options.label: No; the work exceeds the remaining row allowance
options.feedback: Putting the readings into one HTTP message does not reduce how many predictions the model must make. The row allowance still applies to the whole batch.

options.label: Yes; the HTTP request count increased only once
options.feedback: That is the assumption the larger batch exposes.

connections.why: A caller’s identity and resource state cannot come from a model’s untrusted claim.

connections.skill: Keep retries inside an operation budget
connections.why: Repeated calls and batches participate in the same resource accounting.

reflection.prompt: Which information does a label-only interface still reveal to repeated callers?
reflection.carryForward: Keep access, admitted work and public response detail as explicit service policies.

preparation.title: Construct admission before exposing output
preparation.challenge: Require the batch to fit both remaining caller rows and remaining estimated compute units.
preparation.why: A response projector should consume the completed admission decision, not invent its own quota policy.
hints: The remaining caller allowance and new batch size must use the same row unit.
The second branch compares compute units, so calculate the batch’s estimated cost before its Threshold gate.

simulation-time-steps.premise: A larger timestep makes a simple cooling simulator generate impossible-looking training trajectories.

construction.title: Expose the numerical update
construction.start: Build the cooling rate from excess temperature, multiply by elapsed step, and update state.
construction.outcome: The source of the overshoot is visible in the arithmetic.
hints: Cooling depends on how far the current temperature is above ambient. Recalculate that excess for the current state.
Turn that excess into a cooling rate, apply the step duration, and update the temperature. A coarse step can cross ambient even though the exact cooling model would approach it without crossing.

investigation.title: The timestep triples
investigation.question: Does the value below ambient establish a new physical effect?
investigation.outcome: Return to a shorter step before training a surrogate on the trajectory.

options.label: No; the coarse Euler step overshoots
options.feedback: The exact model approaches ambient without this crossing from above.

options.label: Yes; the simulator is always ground truth
options.feedback: A numerical approximation can create behavior absent from the model it approximates.

connections.skill: Interpret a derivative as a local rate
connections.why: We now use that local rate to construct a finite numerical update.

reflection.prompt: What comparison separates numerical error from a wrong cooling law?
reflection.carryForward: Check timestep convergence separately from validation against measured equipment.

simulation-paired-trials.premise: An easier simulated shift made a candidate look better before its policy changed.

construction.title: Pair the policy outcomes
construction.start: Subtract costs on aligned scenarios before taking a mean.
construction.outcome: The comparison describes changes on shared conditions.
hints: Each candidate cost must be compared with the baseline on the same simulated shift. Mixing shifts would mix policy effects with easier conditions.
Keep baseline-minus-candidate gains separate until the final mean. A candidate that costs more on a shift must retain its negative gain.

investigation.title: The unusual shift becomes more expensive
investigation.question: Predict mean gain while keeping the negative gain for the unusual shift.
investigation.outcome: Inspect the regression before deciding whether the average meets the policy requirements.

connections.why: The same comparison now follows complete simulated shifts rather than individual static predictions.

reflection.prompt: Which randomness can genuinely be shared when actions change the future?
reflection.carryForward: State the coupling and reserve fresh scenarios for assessment.

simulation-system-identification.premise: The simulator’s structure is plausible, but its gain does not match the measured conveyor.

construction.title: Estimate the unknown parameter
construction.start: Keep command-response agreement and command energy on separate dot-product branches.
construction.outcome: The fitted value is tied to measured excitation rather than a guessed constant.
hints: The fitted gain should explain all command-response pairs together under the stated through-origin model. It is not the average response or the average of separate response-to-command ratios.
Use the dot product of commands with responses on one branch and commands with themselves on the other. Their ratio fits the shared gain when the commands contain nonzero excitation.

investigation.title: One response changes from four to five
investigation.question: Predict the fitted gain for commands [1,2] and responses [2,5].
investigation.outcome: The fit becomes 2.4; it does not match both observations exactly.

connections.why: We now learn a parameter inside a declared system model.

connections.skill: Fit a relationship from paired measurements
connections.why: The fit is restricted to a physically motivated through-origin form.

reflection.prompt: What residual pattern would suggest a delay instead of a wrong gain?
reflection.carryForward: Use failed predictions to question model structure as well as parameter values.

simulation-transfer-checks.premise: A policy trained on default conditions fails when friction changes.

construction.title: Keep the difficult condition visible
construction.start: Calculate the mean tested cost and the largest tested cost on separate branches. Return them in that order so the individual-condition requirement can be considered beside the average.
construction.outcome: Average improvement cannot erase the worst observed condition.
hints: An ordinary average can hide a difficult condition. Keep the mean and the worst tested cost visible separately.
Build a mean branch and a maximum branch from the same cost list, returning them in that order. A maximum over these tested conditions cannot establish safety in every untested environment.

investigation.title: One condition becomes much harder
investigation.question: Does a mean below eight allow us to ignore the cost of twelve?
investigation.outcome: Preserve the failure for development, then test the repaired policy on a new condition.

options.label: No; inspect the independent condition requirement
options.feedback: The low-friction case fails even if an aggregate seems acceptable.

options.label: Yes; the mean is the whole deployment
options.feedback: The deployment weighting and hard requirements must be justified separately.

connections.why: The learned system parameter may change when the operating condition changes.
Repeated scenario evidence helps separate a condition failure from sampling variation.

reflection.prompt: Which real-world mechanism is missing from the simulator entirely?
reflection.carryForward: Validate the simulator and reserve fresh conditions before claiming transfer.

numerical-stable-normalisation.premise: A new encoder changes numerical scale and breaks the normalization Botie used for retrieval.

construction.title: Protect the products before they are formed
construction.start: Start from the vector-length calculation. Find a common scale before its squares, then check that the resulting direction survives the encoder’s larger values.
construction.outcome: The direction stays the same across a large change in magnitude.
hints: Which single positive number could bring every nonzero component into a manageable range without changing their proportions? Try the largest absolute component.
After rescaling, calculate the remaining length and divide by it. Use the nonzero-divisor tool only to handle actual zero divisors, so a zero vector remains zero.

investigation.title: The first length calculation becomes infinite
investigation.question: Which part of the earlier construction lost the direction?
investigation.outcome: Repair the calculation before interpreting the retrieval result.

options.label: The squares overflowed before the final division
options.feedback: The original components were finite. Changing their scale before multiplying avoids that intermediate failure.

options.label: Every large embedding must have zero relevance
options.feedback: Numerical failure is not evidence about whether a document answers the question.

connections.why: We preserve that same geometric comparison while changing its numerical evaluation.

reflection.prompt: What other failure could remain even after every output direction has length one?
reflection.carryForward: Keep encoder compatibility and retrieval relevance as separate checks from numerical range.

numerical-identifiable-models.premise: The fitted simulator uses two heater gains that the original combined measurements never identified.

construction.title: Construct a test of the competing fits
construction.start: Apply each proposed setting row to both candidate gain vectors. Keep their predictions aligned so that a gap belongs to the experiment that produced it.
construction.outcome: The suggested experiments are tied to a specific unresolved parameter difference.
hints: Both branches must use the same candidate experiment rows and the same coordinate order.
Subtract the two prediction vectors before taking absolute values. Compare those gaps with the planning resolution, then retain passing original positions.

investigation.title: The next batch runs the heaters together again
investigation.question: Did the larger record count resolve which heater contributes more?
investigation.outcome: Design a new measurement that can distinguish the fitted explanations.

options.label: No; both candidates still predict the same totals
options.feedback: These new rows repeat the same combination of inputs. More records need not add an independent direction.

options.label: Yes; every extra row identifies another parameter
options.feedback: Repeated dependent rows can leave the same ambiguity.

connections.why: A returned parameter estimate now needs a check that the experiments could determine it.

connections.skill: Apply one coefficient vector to many rows
connections.why: The same matrix calculation compares candidate predictions at proposed experiments.

reflection.prompt: If a new measurement rejects both candidates, what assumptions would you inspect?
reflection.carryForward: Preserve model alternatives and measurement resolution when planning new evidence.

numerical-gradient-checks.premise: Botie’s symmetric gradient check conceals an absolute-loss corner behind a zero.

construction.title: Keep the two local comparisons separate
construction.start: Build the weight values on each side and evaluate the same loss at all of them. Keep the left and right slopes visible before forming their central average.
construction.outcome: The report explains why a central zero can have different meanings.
hints: Build weight-minus-step and weight-plus-step before evaluating the loss. Each loss machine uses the same target and kind.
The left slope uses center-minus-left; the right uses right-minus-center. Their average is the central difference, which must not replace the separate evidence.

investigation.title: The loss changes to absolute error at its target
investigation.question: Does the central zero establish a classical derivative of zero?
investigation.outcome: Retain both sides before judging the implementation’s derivative convention.

options.label: No; inspect the opposite one-sided slopes
options.feedback: The two sides approach different slopes at this corner.

options.label: Yes; a central estimate always proves differentiability
options.feedback: Symmetric cancellation can hide a nondifferentiable point.

connections.why: We now approximate that local relationship from evaluations of the running program.
An independent finite-difference fixture helps diagnose a reported derivative without replacing training.

reflection.prompt: Which changes to randomness or state would make these perturbations compare different losses?
reflection.carryForward: Keep the loss definition, numerical scale and derivative convention attached to a gradient-check result.

numerical-adaptive-steps.premise: The simulator’s old fixed timestep misses a rapid change that its learned training target must represent.

construction.title: Build an acceptance test around the old update
construction.start: Start with the existing Euler update. Add a branch that evaluates the rate again at a midpoint, then compare both routes before accepting either result.
construction.outcome: A failed attempt has a visible numerical reason rather than silently entering the training trajectory.
hints: The fine branch must take its second half step from the midpoint output, not from the original state again.
Compute the error magnitude and tolerance on separate branches. For Threshold gate, supply tolerance first and error second so acceptance means the allowance is at least the estimate.

investigation.title: The proposed interval grows from a tenth of a second to one second
investigation.question: Will the discrepancy remain inside the same absolute-plus-relative tolerance?
investigation.outcome: The larger interval is rejected. Retry it from the unchanged starting state.

connections.why: The same update becomes a component inside a check of its local approximation.

connections.skill: Keep the procedure that produced training records
connections.why: Solver method and tolerance belong beside the simulator version and generated data.

reflection.prompt: What separate evidence would tell us whether the physical cooling law is wrong?
reflection.carryForward: Track local numerical acceptance separately from complete-trajectory error and agreement with measured equipment.
